meaning: Lists things that happen one after another: “what with A and B, (it was awful)”. Usually has a complaining, exasperated tone.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + わ, verb / i-adjective plain form + わで

senses.label: When it rains, it pours
senses.meaning: Lists several bad things that happen at once or in a row. The second half is usually an overall judgment like 「大変だ」 or 「散々だ」. The tone is “what bad luck, I've had enough”.
senses.connection: A plain form + わ, B plain form + わで, ... (common: 降るわ, 吹くわ, なくすわ, 遅れるわ)
examples: What with the rain and the wind, the trip was a disaster.
I lost my wallet and missed my train. What a terrible day.
My kid has a fever and work is busy, so I don't even have time to rest.

senses.label: Over the top
senses.meaning: The same or similar verbs are repeated to show an action going on and on to an amazing degree. It isn't always bad; it often describes a lively or chaotic scene.
senses.connection: Dictionary form + わ + dictionary form + わで (食べるわ飲むわで, 泣くわわめくわで)
examples: At the year-end party, everyone ate and drank and made a huge racket.
The lost child cried and screamed, and nobody could calm him down.

notes: 「わ」follows the plain form. Verbs cannot take the ます-form, and nouns and na-adjectives need 「だ」: ✕「雨が降りますわ、風が吹きますわで」→ ○「雨は降るわ、風は吹くわで」.
「で」marks a cause, so the sentence should end with a summing-up such as 「大変だった」 or 「散々だった」. In speech the final clause can be left unsaid, but in writing do not stop at 「〜わで。」.
It has a grumbling, complaining tone, so avoid it when explaining a situation formally to a boss or client. For reports, use something plainer such as 「トラブルが続き、対応に追われました」.

Do not treat it as a neutral list. 「〜たり〜たり」can calmly describe a plan, while 「〜わ〜わで」carries strong feelings of “I've had it” or “what a commotion”: ✕「週末は買い物するわ映画を見るわで過ごす予定です」→ ○「週末は買い物したり映画を見たりする予定です」.

daily.title: Complaining to a friend
daily.description: Back from a trip, you complain to a friend about all your bad luck.
daily.example: The flight was late and my luggage got lost. I'm exhausted.

daily.title: Describing a party
daily.description: Telling your family how lively yesterday's party was.
daily.example: Yesterday everyone sang and danced. It was a blast.

daily.title: After moving house
daily.description: Chatting with a neighbor about the chaos on moving day.
daily.example: On moving day it rained and the truck didn't show up. It was rough.

work.title: Chatting about overtime
work.description: At the end of the month, you chat with a coworker about recent trouble at work. Casual office talk.
work.example: This month problems kept popping up and deadlines piled up, so I didn't get any rest.

etymology: The 「わ」 is thought to come from the sentence-final particle 「わ」, which adds emotion or emphasis. Repeating 「〜わ〜わ」 “sighs out” each event one by one, and the 「で」 of cause or state is added, giving “what with A and B, (the result was ...)”.

similar.title: 〜わ〜わ
similar.explanation: Same origin: this pattern is simply 「〜わ〜わ」 plus 「で」. 「〜わ〜わ」 can stand at the end of a sentence as an exclamation (「出るわ出るわ、ゴミの山だ」); once 「で」 is added it marks a cause, and a summarizing result must follow.

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both list several things and hint at a mess. 「〜やら〜やら」 is more neutral and can also list mixed feelings (「嬉しいやら恥ずかしいやら」); 「〜わ〜わで」 is more colloquial and mostly describes a run of bad luck or a chaotic scene.

similar.title: 〜だの〜だの
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: it also lists things with dissatisfaction. 「〜だの〜だの」 mostly lists what someone said or demanded, or trivial matters (「疲れただの眠いだのと文句ばかり言う」); 「〜わ〜わで」 lists events that actually happened one after another.

similar.title: 〜わ (sentence-final particle)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the 「わ」 here is generally thought to come from the sentence-final particle 「わ」 of exclamation. On its own, 「〜わ」 is a soft, feminine assertion in standard Japanese; 「〜わ〜わで」 is used by men and women alike and expresses listing.

formation: It is built by repeating 「plain form + わ」 twice and then adding 「で」, which marks a cause or state. 「わ」 is originally a sentence-final particle of exclamatory assertion: each time you name something you “sigh” once, so two 「〜わ」 throw out the events one after another and create a piled-up “what with this, and what with that” feeling. The final 「で」 bundles the heap into a single cause and leads into a summary such as 「大変だった」 or 「大騒ぎだった」. Because 「わ」 itself is emotional, the whole pattern takes on a tone of complaint or amazement. When the same verb is repeated (「食べるわ飲むわ」), what is being “sighed over” is the sheer amount of the action, which gives the “going on and on, over the top” sense.

meaning: Lists one thing or demand after another: “now it's A, now it's B”. Usually sounds fed up or annoyed.
connection: やれ + noun (だ), やれ + noun (だ) と / だの

senses.label: One thing after another
senses.meaning: Lists events or activities that keep coming: “first it's A, then it's B”. It suggests there's too much to handle and sounds weary.
senses.connection: やれ + noun + だ, やれ + noun + だと (やれ会議だ、やれ出張だと)
examples: What with meetings one day and business trips the next, my father always looks busy.
At the end of the year, what with year-end parties and the big cleanup, I never get to relax.

senses.label: Nagging demands
senses.meaning: Lists someone's various demands, complaints, or excuses: “first they want A, then B”. Often used with 「だの」 or 「と」 and shows the speaker's annoyance.
senses.connection: やれ + noun / plain form + だの, やれ + noun / plain form + だのと (言う, うるさい)
examples: My mom keeps nagging me: “Study!”, “Go to bed early!”
She's always complaining: she's cold, she's hungry.
The customer started complaining that the food was slow and the taste was bland.

notes: It has a clear tone of weariness and nagging. Using it to describe someone's demands in front of them is a direct complaint and very rude (「やれ資料だ、やれ会議だと、部長はうるさい」); use it only when venting to family or friends.

Do not confuse it with the interjection 「やれやれ」: 「やれやれ、やっと終わった」 means “Phew, it's finally over” and expresses relief. In this pattern, 「やれ」 is placed before each listed item, with content between them.
「やれ」 goes before each item and 「やら」 goes after each item; do not mix them up: ✕「会議やれ、出張やれで忙しい」→ ○「やれ会議だ、やれ出張だと忙しい」／○「会議やら出張やらで忙しい」.

daily.title: Complaining about parents
daily.description: A teenager complains to a friend that their parents are too strict.
daily.example: My parents are so annoying: curfew this, grades that.

daily.title: Talking about a child's demands
daily.description: Parents chat about kids always wanting things.
daily.example: My kid keeps asking for a video game, then for comics. It's exhausting.

work.title: Reading an essay
work.description: An essay or column describing how busy modern people are.
work.example: What with work and social obligations, people today have no time for themselves.

work.title: Chatting with a coworker
work.description: A coworker complains about a client's many change requests.
work.example: That client is so demanding: change the design, move up the deadline.

etymology: 「やれ」 was originally a call or exclamation (like 「やあ」 or 「それ」). It is thought to have come to introduce each item in a list. Repeating 「やれ〜やれ〜」 sounds like ticking off complaints one by one, which gives it a fed-up tone.

similar.title: 〜だの〜だの
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: it also lists things with dissatisfaction, and is often combined with this pattern (「やれ〜だの、やれ〜だの」). 「だの」 goes after each item and can be used alone; 「やれ」 goes before each item and gives a stronger feeling of things popping up one after another.

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜やら〜やら」 goes after the items, is more neutral, and can also list complex feelings (「嬉しいやら悲しいやら」); 「やれ〜やれ〜」 goes before the items and is used almost only for irritated nagging.

similar.title: 〜わ〜わで
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both say things come one after another and are too much to bear. 「〜わ〜わで」 follows plain-form verbs and lists bad things that actually happened; 「やれ〜やれ〜」 mostly follows nouns or imperatives and is often used to list other people's demands and tasks piling in.

formation: It is formed by the interjection 「やれ」 plus a listed item (usually 「noun + だ」 or an imperative), repeated two or more times and closed with 「と」 or 「だの」. 「やれ」 was originally a cry used to urge someone on, like “Hey! Come on!”. Put before each item, it sounds as if you are grumbling and shouting out “Hey, now it's this; hey, now it's that...”. The repetition itself conveys “it never ends, I'm sick of it”, so the pattern naturally carries a tone of annoyance. Adding 「だ」 after an item or using an imperative (「勉強しろ」) reproduces the scene or someone's words as they were, and the final 「と」 works like a quotation: “(saying/making a fuss) this and that”. That is why it suits describing someone's nagging demands and a flood of tasks.

meaning: Sentence-final particles that add emphasis. 「ぞ」 is used to psych yourself up or to warn someone; 「ぜ」 is used to assert something or invite someone forcefully.
connection: Plain form + ぞ / ぜ (nouns and na-adjectives can attach directly or as 「だぞ／だぜ」)

senses.label: Psyching yourself up
senses.meaning: Said to yourself to get motivated or make up your mind, like “All right, let's do this!”. Often with 「よし」 or 「さあ」.
senses.connection: Dictionary form / volitional form + ぞ (行くぞ, 頑張るぞ, やるぞ)
examples: All right, today I'm really going to give it my all!
OK, let's go.

senses.label: Reminding / warning
senses.meaning: Emphasizes something to the listener as a reminder or warning: “I'm telling you ...”. Forceful and mainly masculine; not used to superiors or elders.
senses.connection: Plain form + ぞ (危ないぞ, 遅れるぞ, 知らないぞ)
examples: Hurry up or you'll be late.
Hey, it's dangerous over there.
If you lie to me, I won't forgive you.

senses.label: Friendly assertion
senses.meaning: 「ぜ」 is used with close friends to state an opinion or make an invitation forcefully. It sounds breezy and a bit rough. It feels more directed at the listener than 「ぞ」.
senses.connection: Plain form + ぜ; volitional form + ぜ (行こうぜ, やろうぜ)
examples: Come on, let's get started.
This ramen is awesome.

notes: Do not use it to superiors, clients or elders. In modern Japanese, adding 「ぞ」 or 「ぜ」 after the polite form (「明日は早いですぞ」「行きましょうぜ」) sounds comical or arrogant, so do not put them at the end of polite sentences.
Said to another person, 「ぞ」 sounds like a warning or scolding: 「遅れるぞ」 can sound like a threat. Between friends, a kind reminder is gentler with 「遅れるよ」. Women generally do not use it in conversation.
「ぜ」 has a tough-guy flavor, and in real life it tends to sound affected, appearing mostly in the lines of manga and anime characters. Learners should not imitate it.
After a noun or na-adjective, add 「だ」: ✕「本当ぞ」→ ○「本当だぞ」; ✕「静かぜ」→ ○「静かだぜ」.

daily.title: Hurrying the family in the morning
daily.description: A father tells his kid to hurry up and get out the door.
daily.example: It's already eight o'clock. Get up!

daily.title: Inviting friends out
daily.description: Guys making plans to hang out.
daily.example: Let's go to the beach this weekend.

daily.title: Watching manga or anime
daily.description: A hot-blooded hero psyches himself up before a fight.
daily.example: I am absolutely not going to lose!

work.title: Sports practice
work.description: A coach or captain shouts to the team. Typical of sports or on-site work.
work.example: Five more minutes! Run to the end!

etymology: 「ぞ」 comes from the classical emphatic particle 「ぞ」 (as in the 「〜ぞ〜ける」 construction), which later moved to the end of the sentence for emphasis. 「ぜ」 is thought to be a contraction of forms like 「ぞえ」 in Edo-period speech. It was once used by everyone but later became masculine.

similar.title: 〜よ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both convey information to the listener forcefully. 「よ」 is used by men and women, sounds gentle, and can follow the polite form (「遅れますよ」); 「ぞ」 and 「ぜ」 are harsher, strongly masculine, and attach only to the plain form.

similar.title: 〜さ (sentence-final particle)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are colloquial particles that make a declaration. 「さ」 has a casual, “of course” tone (「平気さ」); 「ぞ」 and 「ぜ」 strongly stress, assert or warn.

similar.title: 〜わ (sentence-final particle)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are sentence-final particles that reinforce an assertion, and are often compared as women's and men's speech. In standard Japanese 「わ」 is a soft feminine assertion (「行くわ」), while 「ぞ」 and 「ぜ」 are forceful masculine ones (「行くぞ」「行くぜ」).

formation: This grammar point is a sentence-final particle attached directly to the plain form at the end of a sentence, and its effect comes from that position: it lands “a hammer blow on the whole sentence”. 「ぞ」 comes from the classical emphasizing particle 「ぞ」, which originally pointed out “it is precisely this one”. Moved to the end of the sentence, it emphasizes the whole content: said to oneself it is a resolution (「やるぞ」), and said to someone else it becomes a warning, “I'm telling you” (「危ないぞ」). 「ぜ」 is generally thought to be a contraction of 「ぞえ」 and has an added element of addressing the listener, so it is more “aimed at the other person” than 「ぞ」 and suits invitations and assertions (「行こうぜ」). Both only push the speaker's own judgment without regard for the listener's feelings, so they normally attach only to the plain form and do not go with the polite form.

meaning: Shows that something isn't limited to one person, region, or field, but reaches much further: “not just ... (but also ...)”. Written language.
connection: ひとり + noun + のみならず / だけでなく / にとどまらず

senses.label: Not merely ...
senses.meaning: First names one thing, then says the problem or effect reaches a wider scope. 「ひとり」 stresses “just this one”. Formal; used for social issues and commentary.
senses.connection: ひとり + noun + のみならず, 〜も / 〜全体 (ひとり日本のみならず, ひとり若者だけでなく)
examples: Environmental problems are not Japan's alone but a challenge for the whole world.
This recession is affecting not only small and medium businesses but large companies too.
The falling birthrate is serious not only in rural areas but in cities as well.

senses.label: Not just a problem of ...
senses.meaning: Forms like 「ひとり〜の問題ではない」 or 「ひとり〜にとどまらない」 reject the view that something concerns only one party and stress that it involves everyone.
senses.connection: ひとり + noun + の問題ではない / にとどまらない
examples: Bullying is not just a school problem but a problem for society as a whole.
Its impact goes beyond the industry itself.

notes: 「ひとり」 is an adverb meaning “only, solely”, and it is followed by a noun such as a person, country or organization. It has nothing to do with “one person”: 「ひとり日本のみならず」 does not mean “Japan alone as one person”. Do not write it as 「一人」, and do not add 「で」.
「ひとり」 must be paired with a negating, limiting expression such as 「のみならず」, 「ではない」 or 「にとどまらない」; it cannot stand alone: ✕「これはひとり日本の問題だ」→ ○「これはひとり日本の問題ではない」.
This is a solemn written style used in editorials and speeches. In everyday conversation, saying 「ひとり日本のみならず」 sounds like making a speech; in speech, 「日本だけじゃなくて」 is enough.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news commentator discusses a social issue.
daily.example: Rising prices are squeezing not only household budgets but businesses as well.

daily.title: Reading an editorial
daily.description: An editorial urges people to care about the aging population.
daily.example: An aging society is not a problem for the elderly alone.

work.title: Writing a report
work.description: A research report points out how widespread a problem is.
work.example: The labor shortage is not just our company's issue; it has become a challenge for the entire industry.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: A paper explains how common a phenomenon is.
work.example: This tendency is seen not only in Japanese but in many other languages.

etymology: 「ひとり」 is written 「独り」 and originally means “alone, single”. As an adverb it came to mean “merely, solely”, and is often followed by a negative or 「のみならず」. 「のみならず」 is the limiting particle 「のみ」 plus the classical negative 「ならず」 (“is not”), meaning “not only”.

similar.title: 〜のみならず
similar.explanation: Same origin: this pattern is just 「〜のみならず」 with the adverb 「ひとり」 added. On its own, 「〜のみならず」 only means “not only...”; with 「ひとり」, the limit “this one only” is highlighted, so the sense of widening scope is stronger and the tone more solemn.

similar.title: 〜ただ〜のみならず
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning: “not merely...”. 「ひとり」 is mostly followed by a subject such as a person, country or organization; 「ただ」 has a wider range and can also follow a plain form (「ただ安いのみならず、質もいい」).

similar.title: 〜にとどまらず
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: “not limited to..., extending to...”, and it can also be combined with 「ひとり」. 「にとどまらず」 can follow a verb and stresses going beyond a boundary; 「のみならず」 is a simple “not only”.

similar.title: 〜だけでなく
similar.explanation: The common expression with the same meaning. 「〜だけでなく」 can be used in both speech and writing; 「ひとり〜のみならず」 is a solemn written style used in speeches and editorials.

formation: It is formed as the adverb 「ひとり（独り）」 + noun + 「のみならず」. 「ひとり」 originally means “alone, just one”, and as an adverb it means “solely, merely”, first limiting the subject to “this one only”. 「のみ」 limits it once more, “only”, and 「ならず」 is the negative of the classical copula 「なり」 (equivalent to 「ではなく」), which negates that limit. Emphasizing “this one only” twice and then immediately denying it produces a strong sense of expansion, “not just this one”, so the following clause always names a larger scope such as 「世界全体」 or 「社会全体」. 「ひとり〜の問題ではない」 and 「ひとり〜にとどまらない」 have the same “limit first, then negate” structure.

meaning: Takes some event as a good moment to end something you've been doing or to start something new: “taking ... as an opportunity”.
connection: Noun + を潮に (して) / を潮として

senses.label: Taking the chance to stop
senses.meaning: Treats an event as “just the right moment” to end something ongoing, like ending a party, leaving, retiring, or quitting smoking. Usually for decisions you make yourself.
senses.connection: Noun + を潮に + 引退する / やめる / お開きにする (定年を潮に, これを潮に)
examples: With the president's speech as the cue, the party came to an end.
He retired from active work on his sixtieth birthday.
When my child was born, I took the chance to quit smoking.

senses.label: Taking the chance to start
senses.meaning: Can also mean using a moment to start something new or change direction, but there's still often a sense of saying goodbye to the past.
senses.connection: Noun + を潮に (して) + 始める / 転職する / 故郷に帰る
examples: I took my marriage as the moment to move back to my hometown.
I'm going to use this as a chance to make a fresh start.

notes: It is mostly used for “wrapping things up, taking one's leave, withdrawing”. For something that simply happens to start, use 「きっかけ」: ✕「友人の誘いを潮に、テニスを始めた」→ ○「友人の誘いをきっかけに、テニスを始めた」.
It follows a noun. To attach it to a verb, first nominalize with 「の」: ✕「体調を崩したを潮に」→ ○「体調を崩したのを潮に」.

The related word 「潮時」 means “the time to stop”. Saying 「そろそろ潮時ですね」 to a guest at a banquet or visit amounts to urging them to leave, so mind the occasion; when leaving yourself, 「そろそろ失礼します」 is more fitting.

daily.title: Ending a party
daily.description: When a party has gone on for a while, someone takes the chance to suggest wrapping up.
daily.example: It's started raining, so let's call it a night.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A character in a novel uses something as a chance to leave.
daily.example: When the phone rang, he took the chance to get up from his seat.

work.title: Retirement speech
work.description: At a farewell party, someone explains why they're retiring.
work.example: With my reaching retirement age, I have decided to step down from the front line.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on a company pulling out of a business.
work.example: Following this loss, the company withdrew from its overseas business.

etymology: 「潮」 means the tide. 「潮時 (しおどき)」 was the moment of high or low tide, when fishermen and boatmen had to judge when to set out or come back. It came to mean “the right time to do something”. 「〜を潮に」 means “treating ... as that moment”, so it's often used for stopping or ending.

similar.title: 〜をきっかけに
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are “using... as an opportunity”. 「きっかけ」 is a neutral “trigger, start”, often used for beginning something new, and accidental events are fine; 「〜を潮に」 stresses “seeing the right moment and wrapping up”, and is mostly used for ending, leaving or withdrawing.

similar.title: 〜を契機に
similar.explanation: A close, more formal expression. 「〜を契機に」 is mostly used for major turning points in society or organizations (「事故を契機に法律が改正された」); 「〜を潮に」 is mostly used for personal comings and goings, the breaking up of a gathering and the like.

similar.title: 〜を境に
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both take some event as a dividing line. 「〜を境に」 objectively describes the change before and after, and the change may be involuntary (「その日を境に彼は変わった」); 「〜を潮に」 is a person actively seizing the moment and making a decision.

similar.title: 〜を限りに
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: it is also used for endings. 「〜を限りに」 mostly follows a point in time and declares “it ends there” (「今日を限りに禁煙する」); 「〜を潮に」 follows an event and treats it as a good moment to stop.

formation: It is formed from the object particle 「を」 + the noun 「潮」 + the particle 「に」, and is the pattern 「AをBにする」 (take A as B) with 「する」 dropped: 「Aを潮に（して）」 = “take A as the right moment”. Here 「潮」 means 「潮時（しおどき）」: boatmen must pick the moment of the tide to put out to sea or knock off work, and miss it and it is too late. So “taking something as the right tide” means “seizing this good moment to act”. Since the boatman's “right tide” most often means finishing work and heading to shore, this pattern mostly expresses “bringing something to an end, leaving, withdrawing”, and even when it is used for beginning something new it often carries a sense of “saying goodbye to the past”.

meaning: Follows a number to mean “no less than, at least”, stressing how large the amount is. Written language.
connection: Number + を下らない (を下らず)

senses.label: No less than
senses.meaning: The real amount is at least the stated number, and probably more. The speaker wants to stress that it's large. Common in estimates in news and reports.
senses.connection: Number + を下らない (〜人を下らない, 〜億円を下らない)
examples: Damage from this earthquake is estimated at no less than one trillion yen.
No fewer than ten thousand people attended the rally.
This painting is probably worth no less than 500 million yen.

senses.label: Formal linking forms
senses.meaning: 「〜を下らず」 links clauses mid-sentence, and 「〜を下らぬ」 modifies a noun. Same meaning, more formal.
senses.connection: Number + を下らず, ... / を下らぬ + noun
examples: The death toll is no less than a thousand, and the damage is still spreading.
Every year, no fewer than a hundred inquiries come in.

notes: It is homophonous with the adjective 「くだらない」 (“trivial”), so check whether a quantity comes before it: 「千人を下らない」 means “no fewer than a thousand people”, while 「くだらない話」 means “a pointless story”. Mixing them up turns “huge in scale” into “worthless”.
Do not get the direction backward: 「〜を下らない」 means “not below, at least”, not “at most”. 「一万人を下らない」 = ten thousand or more; for “not more than”, say 「〜を上回らない」 or 「〜以下」.
It is used only for surprisingly large numbers; it sounds unnatural with small or everyday quantities: ✕「参加者は三人を下らない」→ ○「参加者は少なくとも三人いる」.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news report on the scale of a disaster or accident.
daily.example: Reportedly, no fewer than a hundred houses burned down in this fire.

daily.title: Talking about a collector
daily.description: Friends talk about someone's art collection.
daily.example: Apparently that guy owns no fewer than a thousand paintings.

work.title: Market research report
work.description: A report estimates the size of a market.
work.example: The number of potential customers in Japan is estimated at no fewer than five million.

work.title: Business news
work.description: A report on a company's losses.
work.example: The cost of this recall is expected to be no less than ten billion yen.

etymology: 「下る (くだる)」 originally means “to go down”, and by extension “(a value) to fall below”. 「〜を下らない」 literally means “doesn't fall below ...”, hence “at least ...”. The adjective 「くだらない」 (“trivial”) comes from the same root, but the meanings have split apart.

similar.title: 〜からある／〜からする／〜からの
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: they also stress a large quantity. 「〜からある」 is mostly used for the weight, length or price of a concrete object (「20キロからある荷物」) and also works in speech; 「〜を下らない」 is mostly used for counted or estimated figures in news and reports.

similar.title: 〜にのぼる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜にのぼる」 says the figure actually “reaches” a large number, mostly a result already counted (「死者は百人にのぼった」); 「〜を下らない」 means “at least”, mostly an estimate (「百人を下らないと見られる」).

similar.title: 〜(quantity)は (at least)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express “at least...”. 「quantity + は」 is an everyday spoken form with no limit on the size of the number (「三時間はかかる」); 「〜を下らない」 is written style, used only for large numbers, and carries a tone of astonishment.

formation: It is formed from the object particle 「を」 + the negative 「下らない」 of the verb 「下る（くだる）」. 「下る」 originally means “go down”, and for numbers it means “fall below (a line)”, with 「を」 marking that reference line. Literally, 「〜を下らない」 is “does not fall below the line of...”, i.e. it treats the stated number as the lower limit: “at least..., possibly more”. The speaker deliberately speaks from the “lower limit” side to stress “even at the least, it's this many”, so it is used only for large numbers and carries a tone of surprise at the quantity. In writing, the pause form is 「〜を下らず」, and before a noun the classical negative 「〜を下らぬ」 is used, with the same meaning.

meaning: Shows that the result is in proportion to what came before: “you get back as much as you put in”. Both sides rise or fall together.

senses.label: You get what you put in
senses.meaning: The effort in the first half and the reward in the second are proportional: “the more you ..., the more ...”. Often about effort or practice and results, with an encouraging tone.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + 分だけ + 結果が出る / うまくなる / 報われる
examples: The effort you put in will always pay off accordingly.
The more you practice, the better you get.
The harder it was, the greater the joy.

senses.label: Making up for it
senses.meaning: Shows that a gap caused by the first half must be made up by the same amount in the second: “as much as you ..., you have to ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + 分 (だけ), 〜なければならない / 取り戻す
examples: I took time off, so tomorrow I have to work that much harder.
I worked overtime to make up for the delay.

notes: 「分」 is read 「ぶん」, not 「ふん」: 「努力した分だけ」 is read 「どりょくしたぶんだけ」. Read as 「ふん」 it would mean “minutes”.
The latter clause must be a result that corresponds “in proportion” to the former, not a one-off result unrelated to amount: ✕「練習した分だけ、試合に勝った」→ ○「練習した分だけ、上手になった」.
「〜の分」 also means “someone's share”, as in 「私の分も買っておいて」 (buy one for me too). This differs from the present pattern, so do not misread it as “proportional”.

daily.title: Encouraging a friend before an exam
daily.description: Your friend is nervous before an exam, so you cheer them up.
daily.example: Everything you studied will count, so you'll be fine.

daily.title: After a workout
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about dieting.
daily.example: If you don't move as much as you eat, you'll gain weight fast.

daily.title: Splitting costs after a trip
daily.description: Friends dividing up expenses.
daily.example: Just pay for what you used.

work.title: A boss encouraging the team
work.description: A manager motivates the team at the start of a project.
work.example: The more time we spend preparing, the more relaxed we'll be on the day.

work.title: Explaining pricing
work.description: Explaining pay-as-you-go pricing to a customer.
work.example: Please pay only for what you actually use.

etymology: 「分 (ぶん)」 originally means “a divided portion, one's share”, and by extension “a corresponding degree”. 「〜た分だけ」 means “as much as the portion you did”, expressing a proportional relationship.

similar.title: 〜ば〜ほど
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: “the more..., the more...”. 「〜ば〜ほど」 looks at proportion and trend of change (「練習すればするほど上手になる」); 「〜た分だけ」 looks at a one-to-one match between the effort already put in and the result, often with an encouraging or “make up for it” tone.

similar.title: 〜に応じて
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express “correspondingly”. 「〜に応じて」 follows a noun and means adjusting according to circumstances or requests (「成績に応じて奨学金を出す」), and is more objective and written; 「〜た分だけ」 follows a verb ta-form and mostly speaks of personal effort and return.

similar.title: 〜だけ (limit)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the 「だけ」 here is the 「だけ」 of quantity and limit. 「できるだけ」 and 「好きなだけ」 mean “as much as possible, as much as you like”; combined with 「分」 it means “equal to the amount done”.

formation: It is formed from the verb ta-form + the formal noun 「分（ぶん）」 + the particle 「だけ」. 「分」 is “a portion set apart”, and after the ta-form it means “the portion already done”, turning an action into a countable “amount”. 「だけ」 expresses quantity or limit, “that much” (the same kind of 「だけ」 as in 「できるだけ」). Together they mean “an amount equal to what was done”, and with a result stated afterward you get a correspondence: “as much as you do, correspondingly that much...”. Because the core is the “portion”, the first part is often an accumulable action (努力, 練習, 休む) and the second part a result that can increase or decrease; it can be used for rewards, and also for “make up as much as was missed”. 「だけ」 can sometimes be omitted.

meaning: Adds an explanation of the reason for what was just said: “The reason is that ...”.
connection: (Previous sentence.) というのも + plain form + からだ

senses.label: Adding a reason
senses.meaning: First state a result or situation, then bring in the cause with 「というのも」. The sentence often ends with 「からだ」 or 「のだ」. Softer than 「なぜなら」; common in narratives and explanations.
senses.connection: 〜。というのも、plain form + からだ / のだ (nouns / na-adjectives: 〜だからだ)
examples: I haven't been sleeping well lately. That's because the construction next door is so noisy.
He's off today. The reason is that he's had a fever since yesterday.
This shop is always crowded. That's because it's cheap.

senses.label: それというのも
senses.meaning: Adding 「それ」 gives 「それというのも」, which points back to the previous sentence more clearly and sounds more formal. Common in writing.
senses.connection: 〜。それというのも、plain form + からだ / のである
examples: The plan ended in failure. This was because preparation was insufficient.
It's no wonder he succeeded. After all, he worked harder than anyone.

notes: What 「というのも」 introduces is the reason, not the result; reverse the order and the meaning falls apart: ✕「隣の工事がうるさい。というのも、よく眠れない」→ ○「よく眠れない。というのも、隣の工事がうるさいからだ」.
The sentence should end with 「からだ」 or 「のだ」 to match. Writing only 「というのも、工事がうるさい。」 sounds unfinished.
When explaining a reason such as being late to a boss or client, opening with 「というのも〜からです」 sounds like arguing or making excuses; it is more fitting to apologize first and then explain with 「実は〜まして」.
The 「というのも」 in 「彼が怒ったというのも無理はない」 means “(that he got angry) too”, with the content directly before it; it is not this sentence-initial pattern.

daily.title: Explaining why you're late
daily.description: Telling a friend why you arrived late.
daily.example: Sorry I'm late. The train stopped, you see.

daily.title: Writing a blog or diary
daily.description: Explaining a recent change in your diary.
daily.example: I've started cooking lately. That's because I got tired of eating out.

work.title: Explaining to your boss
work.description: Reporting that a deadline will slip and why.
work.example: The delivery is likely to be delayed. This is because parts are arriving late.

work.title: Writing an analysis report
work.description: A report analyzes why sales grew.
work.example: Sales exceeded last year's. This is because the new product was well received.

etymology: Made of the quoting 「と」 + 「いう」 + the nominalizer 「の」 + the particle 「も」. Literally “speaking of (this) ...”, it introduces an explanation of the previous statement and pairs with 「からだ」 at the end.

similar.title: なぜなら〜からだ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: it also adds a reason in a new sentence. 「なぜなら」 states “because” directly and is logical, like an argument; 「というのも」 is softer and more narrative, often used to tell how things came about.

similar.title: 〜のは〜からだ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both pair with 「からだ」 to explain a reason. 「〜のは〜からだ」 joins result and reason in one sentence (「遅れたのは雨のせいだ」); 「というのも」 adds the reason in a new sentence after the previous one.

similar.title: 〜というのは
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are built from 「という＋の＋particle」. 「〜というのは」 follows a word to define or explain it (「JLPTというのは日本語能力試験のことだ」); 「というのも」 comes at the start of a sentence to add a reason.

formation: It is formed from the quotation particle 「と」 + 「いう」 + the formal noun 「の」 + the particle 「も」, closed at the end of the sentence with 「からだ」. 「というの」 refers back to the previous statement as “such a thing” (often with 「それ」 added: 「それというのも」), and 「も」 has a topic-raising tone like “as for that...”, so the whole means “if you ask why that is...”. It only does the opening; the part that actually expresses the reason is the 「からだ」 at the end, and the two enclose the reason between them. Because you state the result first and then add the reason in a new sentence, 「というのも」 goes at the start of the second sentence and cannot come after the reason.

meaning: Whenever the first thing happens, the second always follows: “every time ..., without fail”. Describes habits or regular patterns.
connection: Verb dictionary form + と決まって + ...

senses.label: Without fail
senses.meaning: As soon as the first thing happens, the second happens every single time. Often for someone's habits or quirks, or recurring phenomena. The second half is usually present tense or 「〜たものだ」.
senses.connection: Dictionary form + と決まって + verb (酒を飲むと決まって, 雨が降ると決まって)
examples: Whenever my father drinks, he always starts talking about the old days.
Every time it rains, I get a headache without fail.
Right before an exam, I always get an upset stomach.

senses.label: Always when ...
senses.meaning: The adverb 「決まって」 can also go with 「〜時は」, 「〜たびに」, etc., meaning “whenever ..., always ...”.
senses.connection: 〜時は / 〜たびに / 〜日は + 決まって + verb
examples: On Sundays, our family always goes for a walk together.
Whenever she's in trouble, she always calls her mother.

notes: 「いる」 cannot be added after 「決まって」: 「彼が来ると決まっている」 means “it's been decided that he will come”, while 「彼が来ると決まって雨が降る」 means “whenever he comes, it always rains”. With 「いる」 added the meaning is completely different.
The latter clause must be a recurring pattern or habit; it cannot be used for a one-off event: ✕「昨日、駅に着くと決まって雨が降り出した」→ ○「昨日、駅に着くと雨が降り出した」.
The latter clause cannot be a command, request or the speaker's will: ✕「家に帰ると決まって手を洗いなさい」→ ○「家に帰ったら必ず手を洗いなさい」.
Do not confuse it with 「〜に決まっている」: 「勝つに決まっている」 is the subjective judgment “he's sure to win” and has nothing to do with the habit of “every time”.

daily.title: Talking about family habits
daily.description: Telling a friend about your grandfather.
daily.example: Whenever his grandkids visit, my grandpa always gives them pocket money.

daily.title: Grumbling about your health
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about catching colds when seasons change.
daily.example: I always catch a cold when the seasons change.

daily.title: Childhood memories
daily.description: Telling a friend a story from when you were little.
daily.example: As a kid, I always went to my grandma's house every summer vacation.

work.title: Chatting with coworkers
work.description: Complaining about a machine's old problem.
work.example: This copier always jams right when you're in a hurry.

work.title: Writing an analysis report
work.description: Describing a market pattern.
work.example: Whenever the economy slows down, sales of cheap products always go up.

etymology: 「決まる」 means “to be decided, fixed”. Its te-form 「決まって」 works as an adverb meaning “invariably, as usual”. With the conditional 「と」 before it, it gives “whenever ..., invariably ...”.

similar.title: 〜たびに
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: “every time..., ...”, and often interchangeable. 「〜たびに」 follows the dictionary form or 「noun + の」 and focuses on each occasion; 「〜と決まって」 focuses on a “without-exception” pattern, mostly a person's habit or quirk.

similar.title: 〜ごとに
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: “each, every...”. 「〜ごとに」 mostly follows nouns of time or quantity and stresses repetition per unit (「一時間ごとに」「会うごとに」); 「〜と決まって」 follows a verb and highlights that the result inevitably appears once the condition holds.

similar.title: 〜と (conditional)
similar.explanation: Same origin: this pattern is the conditional 「と」 plus the adverb 「決まって」. 「と」 alone can express a general rule or a one-time discovery (「窓を開けると海が見えた」); with 「決まって」 added, it can only be used for recurring habits.

similar.title: 〜に決まっている
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are built from 「決まる」. 「〜に決まっている」 expresses the speaker's subjective conviction “surely...”; 「〜と決まって」 expresses an objective recurring regularity.

formation: It is formed from the conditional conjunctive particle 「と」 + the adverb 「決まって」. 「と」 itself expresses the inevitable condition “as soon as..., ...” (「春になると花が咲く」); 「決まって」 is the te-form of the verb 「決まる（to be fixed）」 used as an adverb, meaning “as usual, fixed every time”. The former gives the condition and the latter stresses that the result never changes, so together they mean “whenever..., without fail...”. Because 「決まって」 describes an already settled pattern, the latter clause can only be a recurring habit or regularity; and the restriction of the 「と」 conditional, whose latter clause cannot be a command or volition, is also kept.

meaning: Shows that something looks one way on the surface but is actually not: “it seems ..., but actually ...”.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form, na-adjective + な, noun + の + ようでいて

senses.label: Seems ... but actually
senses.meaning: The first half is the impression something gives; the second points out the opposite reality. Often paired with 「実は」, 「意外と」, or 「案外」. Has a reflective “when you think about it, it isn't so” feel.
senses.connection: Plain form + ようでいて, 実は / 意外と〜 (簡単なようでいて, 知っているようでいて)
examples: This problem looks easy, but it's actually quite hard.
We think we know ourselves, but we often don't.
He seems laid-back, but he works really fast.

senses.label: Both ... and ...
senses.meaning: Shows that one thing has two seemingly contradictory sides: “it's ..., and yet also ...”. Often used to describe personalities, works of art, or scenery; a literary tone.
senses.connection: Noun + の / na-adjective + な + ようでいて, 〜でもある
examples: That song sounds cheerful, yet somehow it leaves you feeling lonely.
His manner seems cold, but there's kindness in it too.

notes: The latter clause must contradict or differ from the “surface impression” of the former; it cannot be used when the result matches the impression: ✕「この問題は簡単なようでいて、すぐに解けた」→ ○「この問題は簡単なようでいて、実はかなり難しい」.
Connection: add 「の」 after nouns and 「な」 after na-adjectives: ✕「子供ようでいて」→ ○「子供のようでいて」; ✕「静かようでいて」→ ○「静かなようでいて」.
Used to evaluate people (「優しいようでいて冷たい」), it carries a critical sense of “two-faced”, and is rude said to the person or to a boss.
The 「ようで」 in 「元気なようで安心した」 (“he seems well, so I'm relieved”) is inference plus reason with no contrast following; it is not this grammar point.

daily.title: Describing a friend
daily.description: Talking about a friend who seems careless.
daily.example: She seems sloppy, but she notices the little details.

daily.title: Sharing study tips
daily.description: Japanese learners trade thoughts on studying.
daily.example: Keigo looks simple, but it's hard to master.

work.title: Book or film review
work.description: A review analyzes what makes a work special.
work.example: This novel seems like a simple love story, but it contains sharp social criticism.

work.title: Discussing an issue in a meeting
work.description: Explaining that a task is not as easy as it looks.
work.example: This task looks simple, but it actually takes experience.

etymology: Formed from 「ようで」, the continuative form of 「ようだ」 (appearance, comparison), plus 「いて」, the te-form of 「いる」. It means “being in a state of seeming ...”. When followed by a contrast, it gives “it seems ..., but actually ...”.

similar.title: 〜と思いきや／〜かと思いきや
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean the result is the opposite of the impression. 「〜と思いきや」 says the speaker's expectation was upset, mostly about one concrete event (「晴れるかと思いきや雨だった」); 「〜ようでいて」 speaks of the contrast between outside and essence, and can describe a lasting quality.

similar.title: 〜ながら（も） (concessive)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are adversative. The first part of 「〜ながらも」 is a fact that really holds (「狭いながらも楽しい我が家」); the first part of 「〜ようでいて」 only looks that way and may not be so in reality.

similar.title: 〜ようだ・〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: Same origin: this pattern derives from 「ようだ」. 「ようだ」 alone expresses inference or comparison with no contrast; it is only when it becomes 「ようでいて」 that the “looks like..., actually...” contrast appears.

formation: It is formed from 「ようで」, the continuative form of the auxiliary 「ようだ」, + 「いて」, the te-form of 「いる」. 「ようだ」 means “looks like...”, and 「ようでいる」 literally means “being in a state of looking like...”, stressing that this is only an appearance that keeps going; the te-form 「いて」 then connects the sentence onward. In Japanese, what follows 「〜ていて」 is often something contrasting (「知っていて黙っている」 = knowing but staying silent), so the turn “keeps up the look of..., (but in fact)...” arises naturally. It describes one thing that has both a surface side and a real side, so it can also describe apparently contradictory dual natures.

meaning: Shows that an amount reaches a large number: “amounts to, totals as many as”. Can also mean that something comes up as a topic.

senses.label: Amounts to
senses.meaning: An amount or sum reaches a fairly large number, with a feeling of “that many!”. Common for statistics in news and reports.
senses.connection: Number + にのぼる / にのぼった (〜人にのぼる, 〜億円に上る)
examples: The number of dead and injured in this accident reached one hundred.
Total damage is expected to amount to five billion yen.
Sales of this product reach three million units a year.

senses.label: Coming up as a topic
senses.meaning: Used with nouns like 「話題」, 「議題」, or 「口」 to mean “to be brought up, to be put up for discussion”.
senses.connection: 話題 / 議題 / 口の端 / 食卓 + に上る
examples: That matter was put on the meeting's agenda.
His name has been coming up a lot lately.

notes: Only the kanji 「上る」 is correct; do not write 「登る」 or 「昇る」. 「登る」 is climbing a mountain, and 「昇る」 is the sun rising or being promoted. The quantity sense and the topic sense are always written 「上る」 or in kana 「のぼる」.
It is used only for large numbers that the speaker finds “many”, not for small numbers or merely meeting a standard: ✕「参加者は五人にのぼった」→ ○「参加者は五人だった」.
The topic sense combines only with a few nouns such as 「話題」, 「議題」, 「口の端」 and 「食卓」: 「話題にのぼる」 means “to be talked about”, but you cannot say ✕「ニュースにのぼる」 → ○「ニュースになる」.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news report gives disaster statistics.
daily.example: Reportedly, as many as ten thousand residents were evacuated.

daily.title: Talking about a hot topic
daily.description: A friend mentions something everyone's talking about.
daily.example: That drama comes up a lot at my office too.

work.title: Annual report
work.description: A report describes growth in users.
work.example: Membership reached two million as of the end of last fiscal year.

work.title: Meeting minutes
work.description: Recording that an issue was raised for discussion.
work.example: The issue of cost cutting was put on the agenda again.

etymology: 「のぼる」 is written 「上る／昇る」 and originally means “to go up, rise”. From physical rising it extended to an amount “rising to (a value)” and to being “raised (as a topic or agenda item)”.

similar.title: 〜を下らない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both stress a large quantity. 「〜にのぼる」 says the figure actually “reaches” a large number, mostly a firm count; 「〜を下らない」 means “at least...”, mostly an estimate.

similar.title: 〜からある／〜からする／〜からの
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: they also stress a large quantity. 「〜からある」 is mostly used for the weight, length or price of a concrete object (「10キロからある魚」); 「〜にのぼる」 is mostly used for counted figures such as people or amounts of money, and is common in the news.

similar.title: 〜に至る／〜に至って
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express “reaching”. 「〜に至る」 speaks of a situation developing to a certain stage or result (「倒産に至る」) and does not refer only to quantity; 「〜にのぼる」 is used only for quantity or topics.

formation: It is formed from the case particle 「に」, which marks a destination, + the verb 「上る（のぼる）」. 「上る」 originally means “move upward”, and 「に」 marks the endpoint, so 「Aにのぼる」 means “rise all the way up to the height of A”. If you see a number as a scale being stacked upward, 「百人にのぼる」 is “the count climbs all the way to a hundred people”, which naturally carries the exclamation “that many!”. Likewise, imagining a topic or an agenda as a table or stage, 「話題にのぼる」 and 「議題にのぼる」 mean the matter is “put up on the table”, that is, raised and discussed.

meaning: Shows that everything is ready and only the last step remains: “all that's left is to ..., ready to go”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + ばかりになっている

senses.label: Just waiting to ...
senses.meaning: All the other preparations are done, and only the final action is left: “all that's left is to ..., ready to ... any time”. Often with 「あとは」 or 「もう」.
senses.connection: Dictionary form + ばかりになっている / ばかりになっていた (食べるばかり, 出発するばかり)
examples: The food is ready; it just needs to be put on the table.
The packing is done, and all that's left is to leave.
All the documents were ready; they just had to be submitted.

senses.label: Got everything ready
senses.meaning: 「〜ばかりにしてある／しておく」 means deliberately getting things ready so only the last step is left.
senses.connection: Dictionary form + ばかりにしてある / ばかりにしておく
examples: I've got everything ready so all I have to do is change, so I can head out anytime.
I got the pot ready so it only needs to go on the stove.

notes: It can follow only the dictionary form of a verb; with the ta-form it becomes 「〜たばかり」 (just did), the opposite meaning: 「出発するばかりになっている」 means “all that's left is to depart”, while 「出発したばかりだ」 means “has just departed”.

Do not confuse it with 「〜ばかりだ」 (“just keeps getting...”): 「悪くなるばかりだ」 means “it just keeps getting worse”, while 「出かけるばかりになっている」 means “all that's left is to go out”. The key is whether 「になっている」 follows.
「〜んばかりに」 follows the negative stem and is a figurative “as if about to...”, where the action has not actually happened: 「泣かんばかりに頼む」 means “begs as if about to cry”, not “all that's left is to cry”.

daily.title: Getting ready to move
daily.description: Telling a friend the moving prep is all done.
daily.example: Everything's packed in boxes; all that's left is to carry it out.

daily.title: Dinner at home
daily.description: Everything is ready before the family gets home.
daily.example: Dinner just needs to be heated up, so go ahead and eat.

work.title: Before a system launch
work.description: Reporting to your boss on preparations.
work.example: The new system is all set and ready to go live.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report on a new facility about to open.
work.example: The new station building is finished and just waiting to open.

etymology: 「ばかり」 was originally an adverbial particle of “degree, approximate extent” (from the verb 「はかる」, to measure). It came to mean “only, nothing but”. 「〜するばかりになっている」 means “being in a state where only ... remains”, so everything else is done.

similar.title: 〜ばかりだ (just keeps)
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are “dictionary form + ばかり”. 「〜ばかりだ」 means a situation just keeps going in one direction (mostly a bad one); 「〜ばかりになっている」 means only the last step remains and preparations are complete.

similar.title: 〜たばかり
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「ばかり」 follows the ta-form. 「〜たばかり」 means an action has “just been completed”; 「〜ばかりになっている」 follows the dictionary form and means the action is “not yet done, only waiting to be done”, so the direction in time is exactly opposite.

similar.title: 〜んばかりに／〜んばかりの
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「ばかり」 to mean “just short of”. 「〜んばかりに」 is a figure of speech, “as if about to...”, and the action does not actually happen (「泣かんばかりに頼む」); 「〜ばかりになっている」 means things are really prepared and only the action remains.

formation: It is formed from the dictionary form of a verb + the adverbial particle 「ばかり」 + 「になっている」. 「ばかり」 means “only, nothing but what remains”, so 「〜するばかり」 is “only this one thing is left”; 「になる」 expresses becoming some state, and 「ている」 that this state continues. Together: “it has already become a state where only... remains”, implying that all other steps are finished, hence “everything is ready, only... is left”. It follows the dictionary form because the remaining step has not been done yet. If you change it to 「〜ばかりにしてある」, 「する＋てある」 stresses that someone prepared this state on purpose.

meaning: Expresses heartfelt relief or happiness about a situation: “I'm so glad that ..., nothing could be better”.
connection: Verb te-form / i-adjective くて / noun, na-adjective + で + 何よりだ

senses.label: Happy for someone
senses.meaning: Expresses relief that the other person is safe, healthy, or doing well. A common phrase in greetings and letters; sincere and polite.
senses.connection: お元気そうで / ご無事で / お変わりなくて + 何よりです
examples: I'm so glad to see you looking well.
I'm delighted that everyone is doing well.
I'm so glad you liked it.

senses.label: Glad about the outcome
senses.meaning: Relief about how things turned out: “(whatever else happened,) this is what matters most”. Often used for a silver lining.
senses.connection: 無事で / けががなくて / 間に合って + 何よりだ
examples: I was in an accident, but thank goodness I wasn't hurt.
We lost the game, but the main thing is everyone's safe.

notes: It is mainly used to express relief at another person's well-being or good news. Used for your own good fortune (「私が合格して何よりです」), it sounds self-appraising and awkward; say 「合格できてよかったです」 instead.
It can only be used for the good side, never for bad things: ✕「病気になって何よりだ」. When used for “a blessing in disguise”, pick out the good side in the first part: ○「けががなくて何よりだ」.
Saying 「お元気そうで何よりです」 to a boss or client is fitting; in letters the more formal expressions are 「何よりと存じます」 and 「何よりでございます」. A bare 「何より！」 is quite casual.
The adverb 「何より（も）」 (「健康が何より大切だ」 = health is more important than anything) is not this grammar point; this one must be “te-form / 「で」 + 何よりだ”.

daily.title: Seeing someone after a long time
daily.description: Greeting an older relative you haven't seen in ages.
daily.example: Grandma, I'm so glad to see you looking so well.

daily.title: A friend leaves the hospital
daily.description: Calling a friend after they're discharged.
daily.example: I'm so glad you got out of the hospital safely.

work.title: Opening a business email
work.description: A greeting in an email to a client.
work.example: I trust everyone is keeping well, and I am very glad to hear it.

work.title: At the end of a project
work.description: A manager expresses relief that the team finished smoothly.
work.example: I'm glad it all wrapped up without any major problems.

etymology: 「何より」 means “more than anything”, made of the question word 「何」 plus 「より」 of comparison. With a te-form of cause before it, it means “because ..., it's better than anything”, i.e., “I'm so glad that ...”.

similar.title: 〜てよかった
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express “I'm glad that...”. 「〜てよかった」 is the most general and can be used for your own affairs (「合格してよかった」); 「〜て何よりだ」 is more formal and mostly expresses relief about the other person or the situation as a whole.

similar.title: 〜に越したことはない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both imply “... is best”. 「〜に越したことはない」 is a general suggestion or judgment, mostly about something not yet happened (「安いに越したことはない」); 「〜て何よりだ」 expresses relief about a good result that has already come about.

similar.title: 〜限りだ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: it can express intense joy (「嬉しい限りだ」). 「〜限りだ」 directly says that your own feeling has reached its limit; 「〜て何よりだ」 judges the situation as “the best that could be”, in a calmer tone.

formation: It is formed from the causal te-form + 「何より」 + the copula 「だ」. 「何より」 is the interrogative 「何」 + the comparative case particle 「より」, literally “than anything”, with 「良い」 omitted afterward, i.e. “better than anything”. The preceding te-form gives “because...”, and the whole means “because..., this is (better than anything) good”. Since the speaker is judging from a bystander's standpoint that something is “the best”, it naturally carries feelings of relief and gladness, and is often used for another person's well-being or health. In a misfortune, picking out only the good side in the first part turns it into “at least that's a blessing”.
